claim: The peptidoglycan cell wall is a defining structural feature of the bacterial kingdom.
source: The peptidoglycan cell wall is a defining structural feature of the bacterial kingdom.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: Some bacteria have the ability to switch to a wall-free or 'L-form' state.
source: Curiously, some bacteria have the ability to switch to a wall-free or 'L-form' state.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inhibition of peptidoglycan precursor synthesis promotes the generation of L-forms from both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Here we show that inhibition of peptidoglycan precursor synthesis promotes the generation of L-forms from both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 with multiple bacterial species.

claim: L-forms generated have in common a mechanism of proliferation involving membrane blebbing and tubulation.
source: We show that the L-forms generated have in common a mechanism of proliferation involving membrane blebbing and tubulation, which is dependent on an altered rate of membrane synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and Videos 1-4.

claim: L-form proliferation is dependent on an altered rate of membrane synthesis.
source: We show that the L-forms generated have in common a mechanism of proliferation involving membrane blebbing and tubulation, which is dependent on an altered rate of membrane synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing effects of fatty acid synthesis inhibition.

claim: L-form mode of proliferation is independent of the essential FtsZ based division machinery.
source: Crucially, this mode of proliferation is independent of the essential FtsZ based division machinery.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2, Figure 4 showing deletion of ftsZ in L-forms.

claim: The L-form mode of proliferation is conserved across the bacterial kingdom.
source: Our results suggest that the L-form mode of proliferation is conserved across the bacterial kingdom, reinforcing the idea that it could have been used in primitive cells, and opening up its use in the generation of synthetic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar L-form properties across diverse bacterial species.

claim: The L-form mode of proliferation could have been used in primitive cells.
source: Our results suggest that the L-form mode of proliferation is conserved across the bacterial kingdom, reinforcing the idea that it could have been used in primitive cells, and opening up its use in the generation of synthetic cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the conservation of L-form proliferation mechanisms.

claim: The peptidoglycan cell wall is present in all known major bacterial phyla.
source: The peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall is a major defining feature of bacterial cells and is present in all known major bacterial phyla, suggesting that the wall was present in the last common ancestor of the whole bacterial lineage (Errington, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Errington, 2013.

claim: The cell wall was present in the last common ancestor of the whole bacterial lineage.
source: The peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall is a major defining feature of bacterial cells and is present in all known major bacterial phyla, suggesting that the wall was present in the last common ancestor of the whole bacterial lineage (Errington, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Errington, 2013.

claim: PG is composed of long glycan strands cross linked by short peptide bridges, forming a meshwork that covers the whole cell.
source: PG is composed of long glycan strands cross linked by short peptide bridges, forming a meshwork that covers the whole cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure.

claim: The cell wall has functions including maintenance of cell shape, protection from mechanical damage, and generation of turgor.
source: The wall has a variety of important functions, including the following: maintenance of cell shape, protection from mechanical damage, and generation of turgor by restraining the outward osmotic pressure exerted on the cytoplasmic membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell wall functions.

claim: The cell wall is the target for β-lactams and glycopeptide antibiotics.
source: It is the target for our best antibiotics (β-lactams, glycopeptides, etc), and fragments of the wall trigger important innate immune responses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibiotic mechanisms.

claim: Fragments of the cell wall trigger important innate immune responses.
source: It is the target for our best antibiotics (β-lactams, glycopeptides, etc), and fragments of the wall trigger important innate immune responses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about immune system interactions with bacterial cell walls.

claim: The wall is assembled by polymerization and cross linking of lipid II.
source: The wall is assembled by polymerization and cross linking of a precursor molecule, termed lipid II, which is synthesized in the cytoplasm and then transferred to the cell surface for wall assembly (Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Typas et al., 2012.

claim: Lipid II is synthesized in the cytoplasm and then transferred to the cell surface for wall assembly.
source: The wall is assembled by polymerization and cross linking of a precursor molecule, termed lipid II, which is synthesized in the cytoplasm and then transferred to the cell surface for wall assembly (Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Typas et al., 2012.

claim: Many bacteria, both Gram-positives and Gram-negatives, are capable of switching into a cell wall deficient state called the 'L-form'.
source: Despite its importance, many bacteria, both Gram-positives and Gram-negatives, are capable of switching into a cell wall deficient state, called the 'L-form' (Allan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Allan et al., 2009.

claim: L-forms were generally generated under osmoprotective conditions by long term and repeated passage in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics.
source: Generally, L-forms were generated under osmoprotective conditions (e.g. in the presence of 0.5 M sucrose) by long term and repeated passage, sometimes for years, in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics that inhibit PG synthesis (Allan, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Allan, 1991.

claim: When dividing in the L-form state, B. subtilis becomes completely independent of the FtsZ based division machinery.
source: First, that when dividing in the L-form state, B. subtilis becomes completely independent of the FtsZ (tubulin) based division machinery (Leaver et al., 2009) and the MreB (actin) cytoskeleton (Mercier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leaver et al., 2009 and Mercier et al., 2012.

claim: B. subtilis L-forms become independent of the MreB cytoskeleton.
source: First, that when dividing in the L-form state, B. subtilis becomes completely independent of the FtsZ (tubulin) based division machinery (Leaver et al., 2009) and the MreB (actin) cytoskeleton (Mercier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mercier et al., 2012.

claim: L-forms divide by a process of cell shape deformation, including blebbing, tubulation, and vesiculation, followed by spontaneous resolution into smaller progeny cells.
source: Instead, the L-forms divide by a remarkable process of cell shape deformation, including blebbing, tubulation, and vesiculation, followed by spontaneous resolution (scission) into smaller progeny cells (Kandler and Kandler, 1954; Leaver et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kandler and Kandler, 1954 and Leaver et al., 2009.

claim: L-form proliferation in B. subtilis depends on excess membrane synthesis, leading to an increase in the surface area to volume ratio.
source: We recently showed that L-form proliferation in B. subtilis simply depends on excess membrane synthesis, leading to an increase in the surface area to volume ratio (Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mercier et al., 2013.

claim: Upregulation of membrane synthesis can be driven directly by mutations affecting the regulation of fatty acid synthesis.
source: Upregulation of membrane synthesis can be driven directly, by mutations affecting the regulation of fatty acid synthesis, or indirectly, by shutting down PG precursor synthesis, which presumably depends on a regulatory circuit that we do not yet understand.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental findings and inference about mechanisms.

claim: Upregulation of membrane synthesis can be driven indirectly by shutting down PG precursor synthesis.
source: Upregulation of membrane synthesis can be driven directly, by mutations affecting the regulation of fatty acid synthesis, or indirectly, by shutting down PG precursor synthesis, which presumably depends on a regulatory circuit that we do not yet understand.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and speculation about the underlying mechanism.

claim: The growth of B. subtilis L-forms requires a mutation in ispA gene.
source: To complicate matters, the growth of B. subtilis L-forms requires a second mutational change, most commonly affecting the ispA gene (Leaver et al., 2009), which probably works by compensating for a metabolic imbalance that occurs when cells grow in the absence of wall synthesis (Kawai and Mercier, unpublished).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leaver et al., 2009 and unpublished data.

claim: The ispA mutation probably works by compensating for a metabolic imbalance that occurs when cells grow in the absence of wall synthesis.
source: To complicate matters, the growth of B. subtilis L-forms requires a second mutational change, most commonly affecting the ispA gene (Leaver et al., 2009), which probably works by compensating for a metabolic imbalance that occurs when cells grow in the absence of wall synthesis (Kawai and Mercier, unpublished).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on unpublished data.

claim: Inhibition of PG precursor synthesis is lethal on non-osmoprotective nutrient agar plates.
source: Although inhibiting the PG precursor pathway was lethal on non-osmoprotective nutrient agar (NA) plates (lipid II OFF, NA), growth of B. subtilis was restored on osmoprotective NA/supporting medium (MSM) plates (lipid II OFF, MSM), via a switch to an L-form mode of proliferation (Leaver et al., 2009; Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Growth of B. subtilis is restored on osmoprotective NA/MSM plates via a switch to an L-form mode of proliferation when PG precursor synthesis is inhibited.
source: Although inhibiting the PG precursor pathway was lethal on non-osmoprotective nutrient agar (NA) plates (lipid II OFF, NA), growth of B. subtilis was restored on osmoprotective NA/supporting medium (MSM) plates (lipid II OFF, MSM), via a switch to an L-form mode of proliferation (Leaver et al., 2009; Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations.

claim: S. aureus and E. coli are both susceptible to fosfomycin at 400 μg/ml.
source: S. aureus and E. coli were both susceptible to FOS at 400 μg/ml.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: C. glutamicum is resistant to fosfomycin but susceptible to D-cycloserine at 400 μg/ml.
source: C. glutamicum was resistant to FOS but susceptible to DCS at the same concentration.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: Growth of S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli on NA is inhibited in the presence of fosfomycin or D-cycloserine.
source: Figure 1 (D, F, H) shows that the growth of all three strains on NA was inhibited in the presence of the drug (lipid II OFF).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, F, H.

claim: Growth of S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli is efficiently restored under osmoprotective conditions when treated with fosfomycin or D-cycloserine.
source: However, as observed in B. subtilis, growth of all three strains was efficiently restored under osmoprotective conditions (lipid II OFF, MSM).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, F, H.

claim: Phase contrast microscopy of S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli treated cultures revealed the presence of large spheroidal cells similar to B. subtilis L-forms.
source: Furthermore, phase contrast microscopy of the three treated cultures (Figure 1E, G, I; OFF) revealed the presence of large spheroidal cells strikingly similar to the L-forms of B. subtilis (Figure 1C) and quite different from the parental walled cells (Figure 1E, G, I; ON), consistent with the idea that all three diverse organisms are able to switch to an L-form mode of proliferation on inhibition of the PG precursor pathway.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C, E, G, I.

claim: L-forms of S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli can be successively propagated in the presence of high concentrations of β-lactam antibiotics.
source: We further showed that L-forms of the three different species could be successively propagated in the presence of high (500 μg/ml) concentrations of β-lactam antibiotics (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) in concentrations that are normally lethal in walled cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: On reactivation of PG precursor synthesis, S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli L-forms readily reverted to their parental walled forms.
source: Finally, on reactivation of PG precursor synthesis, the three different species readily reverted to their parental walled forms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), by de novo synthesis of the cell wall sacculus (Kawai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B, and citation to Kawai et al., 2014.

claim: L-forms revert to walled forms by de novo synthesis of the cell wall sacculus.
source: Finally, on reactivation of PG precursor synthesis, the three different species readily reverted to their parental walled forms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), by de novo synthesis of the cell wall sacculus (Kawai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kawai et al., 2014.

claim: In B. subtilis, proliferation in the L-form state renders the normally essential genes of the PG precursor pathway dispensable.
source: In B. subtilis, proliferation in the L-form state renders the normally essential genes of the PG precursor pathway dispensable (Leaver et al., 2009; Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leaver et al., 2009 and Mercier et al., 2013.

claim: The murA gene is essential for E. coli growth in the walled state.
source: In walled cells, the presence of plasmid pOU82-murA was essential for growth of strain RM345 (Figure 2A, bottom), as demonstrated by the uniform blue colonies on X-gal, while it was readily lost from the parental TB28 strain (murA+), giving many white colonies (Figure 2A, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The murA gene is dispensable for E. coli growth in the L-form state.
source: Strikingly, the plasmid was also readily lost from strain RM345 when grown in the putatively L-form state, as indicated by the white colonies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: C. glutamicum L-forms undergo repeated shape deformations with proliferative events generating separate cells.
source: Figure 3A and Video 1 and Video 2 show typical time courses. In Figure 3A, the central cell underwent repeated shape deformations, with proliferative events generating separate cells after 200 and 315 min (*).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: E. coli L-forms proliferate by a mode reminiscent of Gram-positive B. subtilis and C. glutamicum L-forms.
source: Figure 3B (and Video 3 and Video 4) show typical examples of an E. coli ΔmurA L-form strain grown on solid medium (NA/MSM). Strikingly, the mode of cell proliferation is reminiscent of the Gram-positive B. subtilis and C. glutamicum L-forms.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: E. coli L-forms undergo a repeat cycle of cell deformation and cell protrusion formation followed by spontaneous division generating progeny cells.
source: We observed a repeat cycle of cell deformation and cell protrusion formation at 105–160 min and 185–200 min (arrows), each followed by a spontaneous division generating progeny cells after 170 min and 205 min (*).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The general features of the L-form mode of cell proliferation are conserved between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
source: It thus appears that the general features of the L-form mode of cell proliferation are conserved between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar proliferation patterns across different bacterial species.

claim: Cell division of walled bacteria requires the assembly and function of a complex proteinaceous machinery built around the essential tubulin homologue FtsZ.
source: Cell division of walled bacteria requires the assembly and function of a complex proteinaceous machinery built around the essential tubulin homologue FtsZ (Adams and Errington, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adams and Errington, 2009.

claim: In B. subtilis L-forms, the FtsZ protein and probably the whole cell division machinery become dispensable.
source: We showed previously that in B. subtilis L-forms, remarkably the FtsZ protein and probably the whole cell division machinery become dispensable (Leaver et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leaver et al., 2009.

claim: FtsZ is essential for E. coli growth in the walled state.
source: When RM349 was grown in the walled state, FtsZ appeared essential, as judged by the blue only colonies (Figure 4A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: FtsZ is dispensable for E. coli growth in the L-form state.
source: Once again, when induced to grow in the L-form state, FtsZ became dispensable, as characterized by the presence of white colonies on X-gal plates (Figure 4B, top left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Both FtsZ and MurA proteins are simultaneously dispensable in E. coli L-forms.
source: Additionally, using a similar strategy, we showed that both FtsZ and MurA proteins were simultaneously dispensable in L-forms (Figure 4B, top right, and Figure 4C lanes 3 and 4), as well as another essential cell division protein FtsK (Figure 3B, bottom left and 4C lanes 5 and 6), and the cytoskeleton proteins MreBCD (Figure 4B, bottom right, and Figure 4C lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: FtsK is dispensable in E. coli L-forms.
source: Additionally, using a similar strategy, we showed that both FtsZ and MurA proteins were simultaneously dispensable in L-forms (Figure 4B, top right, and Figure 4C lanes 3 and 4), as well as another essential cell division protein FtsK (Figure 3B, bottom left and 4C lanes 5 and 6), and the cytoskeleton proteins MreBCD (Figure 4B, bottom right, and Figure 4C lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: MreBCD cytoskeleton proteins are dispensable in E. coli L-forms.
source: Additionally, using a similar strategy, we showed that both FtsZ and MurA proteins were simultaneously dispensable in L-forms (Figure 4B, top right, and Figure 4C lanes 3 and 4), as well as another essential cell division protein FtsK (Figure 3B, bottom left and 4C lanes 5 and 6), and the cytoskeleton proteins MreBCD (Figure 4B, bottom right, and Figure 4C lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: S. aureus L-forms can proliferate independently of FtsZ.
source: However, when the cells were switched into an L-form mode of proliferation (lipid II OFF), no growth difference was detectable between the presence (+FtsZ) or absence (−FtsZ) of IPTG.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: S. aureus L-forms can proliferate in the absence of functional FtsZ protein.
source: In accordance with the above results, growth in the absence of benzamide was restored when the cells were switched to the L-form state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, lipid II OFF), again showing that S. aureus L-forms can proliferate independently of FtsZ and hence of the normal cell division machinery.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cephalexin is a specific inhibitor of the essential cell division protein FtsI.
source: To test the requirement for the cell division machinery in C. glutamicum L-forms, we cultured the organism in the walled and L-form states in the presence of cephalexin, a specific inhibitor of the essential cell division protein FtsI (Pogliano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pogliano et al., 1997.

claim: Cephalexin blocks cell division in normal walled C. glutamicum cells, leading to a severe growth defect.
source: As previously shown, cephalexin blocks cell division in normal walled cells (Valbuena et al., 2006), leading to a severe growth defect (Figure 4E, left and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, middle).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and citation to Valbuena et al., 2006.

claim: In the L-form mode of proliferation, C. glutamicum shows no growth defect in the presence of cephalexin.
source: However, in the L-form mode of proliferation, no growth defect was observed (Figure 4E, right and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, right), again supporting the idea that L-form proliferation is independent of the normal cell division machinery.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A minor reduction in fatty acid synthesis that had no effect on walled cell growth or division specifically abolished B. subtilis L-form proliferation.
source: We recently showed that a minor reduction in fatty acid synthesis, that had no effect on walled cell growth or division, specifically abolished B. subtilis L-form proliferation (Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mercier et al., 2013.

claim: A fabH null strain of E. coli proliferates in the walled state on NA/MSM plates.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, a fabH null strain proliferated in the walled state on NA/MSM plates (lipid II ON), while no growth was detected following a switch to the L-form mode of proliferation (lipid II OFF, middle).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A fabH null strain of E. coli shows no growth in the L-form state.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, a fabH null strain proliferated in the walled state on NA/MSM plates (lipid II ON), while no growth was detected following a switch to the L-form mode of proliferation (lipid II OFF, middle).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The growth defect of fabH null E. coli L-forms is restored by a fabH+ complementing plasmid.
source: Importantly, this growth defect was restored by a fabH+ complementing plasmid (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cerulenin specifically inhibits E. coli L-form proliferation.
source: Similar results were obtained using cerulenin, an antibiotic that inhibits FA synthesis, which specifically inhibited L-form proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In E. coli walled cells, the murA gene is retained but the fabH gene is lost when both are on unstable plasmids.
source: As expected, in the walled state, the murA gene was retained because PG synthesis is essential, but the fabH gene was lost, because E. coli apparently has a second activity capable of supporting the fabH function (Yao et al., 2012) (Figure 5C, lane 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citation to Yao et al., 2012.

claim: In E. coli L-form cells, the murA gene is lost while the fabH gene is retained when both are on unstable plasmids.
source: Strikingly, in the L-form state, the opposite was observed: murA was lost, while fabH was retained (Figure 5C, lane 2), supporting the idea that a higher rate of FA synthesis is required for proliferation of E. coli in the L-form state.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A higher rate of FA synthesis is required for proliferation of E. coli in the L-form state.
source: Strikingly, in the L-form state, the opposite was observed: murA was lost, while fabH was retained (Figure 5C, lane 2), supporting the idea that a higher rate of FA synthesis is required for proliferation of E. coli in the L-form state.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing retention of fabH in L-forms.

claim: E. coli has a second activity capable of supporting the fabH function.
source: As expected, in the walled state, the murA gene was retained because PG synthesis is essential, but the fabH gene was lost, because E. coli apparently has a second activity capable of supporting the fabH function (Yao et al., 2012) (Figure 5C, lane 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yao et al., 2012.

claim: Partial inhibition of FA synthesis with cerulenin specifically inhibits C. glutamicum L-form proliferation.
source: In accordance with the results for E. coli (above), partial inhibition of FA synthesis specifically inhibited L-form proliferation (Figure 5D, left), with no effect on the walled cells (Figure 5D, middle).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Partial inhibition of FA synthesis with cerulenin has no effect on C. glutamicum walled cells.
source: In accordance with the results for E. coli (above), partial inhibition of FA synthesis specifically inhibited L-form proliferation (Figure 5D, left), with no effect on the walled cells (Figure 5D, middle).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the presence of cerulenin, C. glutamicum L-form cells continue to grow but shape deformations do not occur, and cells remain spherical with no detectable division events.
source: Strikingly, in the presence of cerulenin, cells continued to grow but shape deformations did not occur, and the cells remained more or less spherical with no detectable division events (Figure 5E, right, and Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5E and Video 6.

claim: Regulation of membrane synthesis has a pivotal role in the proliferation of diverse Gram-positive and Gram-negative L-forms.
source: Thus, as previously described for B. subtilis L-forms, regulation of membrane synthesis seems to have a pivotal role in the proliferation of diverse Gram-positive and Gram-negative L-forms.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing effects of fatty acid synthesis on L-form proliferation across species.

claim: Historically, L-forms from diverse bacteria were generated using many different cell wall inhibitors.
source: Historically, L-forms from diverse bacteria were generated using many different cell wall inhibitors, such as β-lactams, glycopeptides, and lytic enzymes (Domingue and Woody, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Domingue and Woody, 1997.

claim: The wide range of methods used to create L-forms has contributed to heterogeneity in phenotypic properties.
source: The wide range of methods used to create L-forms has probably contributed to the heterogeneity in phenotypic properties and has made it difficult to define general properties for L-form bacteria (Domingue and Woody, 1997; Allan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the literature and supported by citations.

claim: Some cells designated L-form 'like' have been cell types in which the PG synthesis machinery remained essential for proliferation.
source: Included in the range of cells designated L-form 'like' have been cell types in which the PG synthesis machinery remained essential for proliferation (e.g. the E. coli cells of Joseleau-Petit et al., 2007 and Cambre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joseleau-Petit et al., 2007 and Cambre et al., 2014.

claim: E. coli can be converted into a state in which the cell wall precursor pathway can be deleted and cells become completely resistant to β-lactam antibiotics.
source: Given that we have now shown that E. coli can be converted into a state in which the cell wall precursor pathway can be deleted and cells become completely resistant to β-lactam antibiotics, we suggest that in future the term L-form be restricted to fully wall deficient cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript showing deletion of murA and resistance to antibiotics.

claim: The term L-form should be restricted to fully wall deficient cells.
source: Given that we have now shown that E. coli can be converted into a state in which the cell wall precursor pathway can be deleted and cells become completely resistant to β-lactam antibiotics, we suggest that in future the term L-form be restricted to fully wall deficient cells.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Inhibiting an earlier step of the PG precursor pathway efficiently generates proliferating L-forms in B. subtilis.
source: We previously showed that for B. subtilis, inhibiting an earlier step of the PG precursor pathway efficiently generates proliferating L-forms (Leaver et al., 2009; Dominguez-Cuevas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leaver et al., 2009 and Dominguez-Cuevas et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of the PG precursor pathway has been tried only rarely in previous L-form work.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, this approach appears to have been tried only rarely in previous L-form work (Schmid, 1984, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmid, 1984, 1985.

claim: The PG precursor synthesis pathway is almost ubiquitous in bacteria.
source: Finally, as the PG precursor synthesis pathway is almost ubiquitous in bacteria, it is reasonable that this method could be applied to a very wide range of bacteria.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about bacterial cell wall synthesis.

claim: The method of inhibiting PG precursor synthesis could be applied to a very wide range of bacteria to generate L-forms.
source: Finally, as the PG precursor synthesis pathway is almost ubiquitous in bacteria, it is reasonable that this method could be applied to a very wide range of bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the ubiquity of the pathway and the experimental success with diverse species.

claim: In B. subtilis, PG precursor synthesis inhibition triggers induction of excess membrane synthesis.
source: However, we recently uncovered that in B. subtilis, PG precursor synthesis inhibition triggers, by an unknown mechanism, induction of an excess of membrane synthesis, a key process for L-form cell division (Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mercier et al., 2013.

claim: PG synthesis needs to be coordinated either with membrane synthesis or cell growth.
source: Thus, as PG synthesis needs to be coordinated either with membrane synthesis or cell growth, it is plausible that PG precursor synthesis inhibition has general effects on the regulation of membrane synthesis in bacteria.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and inference about cellular coordination.

claim: PG precursor synthesis inhibition may have general effects on the regulation of membrane synthesis in bacteria.
source: Thus, as PG synthesis needs to be coordinated either with membrane synthesis or cell growth, it is plausible that PG precursor synthesis inhibition has general effects on the regulation of membrane synthesis in bacteria.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed effects and known cellular coordination.

claim: B. subtilis L-forms can proliferate in both solid and liquid media.
source: We previously found that B. subtilis L-forms can proliferate in both solid and liquid media (Leaver et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leaver et al., 2009.

claim: C. glutamicum L-forms can proliferate under both solid and liquid conditions.
source: Interestingly, although C. glutamicum L-forms shared the ability to proliferate under both conditions, S. aureus and E. coli L-forms only grew on an agar surface.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: S. aureus and E. coli L-forms only grow on an agar surface.
source: Interestingly, although C. glutamicum L-forms shared the ability to proliferate under both conditions, S. aureus and E. coli L-forms only grew on an agar surface.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: L. monocytogenes L-forms grow only under semi-solid conditions.
source: Another recently characterized L-form, from the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes, was also reported to grow only under semi-solid conditions (Dell'Era et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dell'Era et al., 2009.

claim: The ability of L-forms to proliferate under different growth conditions is dependent on as yet unknown inherent properties of each bacterial species.
source: Thus the ability of L-forms to proliferate under different growth conditions is dependent on as yet unknown inherent properties of each bacterial species.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in growth conditions across species.

claim: L-form proliferation in B. subtilis requires a mutation in ispA in addition to inhibition of PG precursor synthesis.
source: We previously showed that L-form proliferation in B. subtilis requires, in addition to inhibition of PG precursor synthesis, a mutation in a gene such as ispA (Leaver et al., 2009; Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leaver et al., 2009 and Mercier et al., 2013.

claim: In the absence of an ispA mutation, no growth is detected in B. subtilis on inhibition of PG precursor synthesis.
source: In the absence of such a mutation, no growth is detected on inhibition of PG precursor synthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli readily proliferate on inhibition of PG precursor synthesis without requiring an ispA-like mutation.
source: Interestingly, the different bacteria tested here readily proliferated on inhibition of PG precursor synthesis, strongly suggesting that no ispA-like mutation is needed to promote L-form proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing L-form growth without additional mutations.

claim: The requirement for a secondary mutation to promote L-form proliferation depends on the bacterium tested.
source: Thus it appears again that the requirement for a secondary mutation to promote L-form proliferation will depend on the bacterium tested.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences observed between B. subtilis and other bacteria.

claim: FtsZ independent proliferation is a common trait of bacterial L-forms.
source: Thus FtsZ independent proliferation is a common trait of bacterial L-forms, presumably reflecting their strange blebbing/tubulation mode of growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing FtsZ dispensability across multiple species.

claim: The ability to tolerate deletion of essential cell division genes such as ftsZ is a useful operational test for the true L-form state.
source: We suggest that the ability to tolerate deletion of essential cell division genes such as ftsZ will be a useful operational test for the true L-form state.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: B. subtilis L-forms are able to synthesize a cell wall sacculus de novo, followed by reversion to the parental walled form.
source: We recently showed that B. subtilis L-forms are able to synthesis a cell wall sacculus de novo, followed by reversion to the parental walled form (Kawai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kawai et al., 2014.

claim: After reactivating PG precursor synthesis, S. aureus, C. glutamicum, and E. coli L-forms can revert to their parental walled forms.
source: Similarly, after reactivating PG precursor synthesis by removal of FOS or DCS, the three different bacterial L-forms tested here could also revert to their parental walled forms, suggesting that the ability to rebuild a cell wall sacculus de novo is also a common property of bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ability to rebuild a cell wall sacculus de novo is a common property of bacteria.
source: Similarly, after reactivating PG precursor synthesis by removal of FOS or DCS, the three different bacterial L-forms tested here could also revert to their parental walled forms, suggesting that the ability to rebuild a cell wall sacculus de novo is also a common property of bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reversion across multiple species.

claim: C. glutamicum and E. coli L-forms proliferate by cell shape deformations followed by spontaneous scission events.
source: We reported here that C. glutamicum and E. coli L-forms, at least, appear to proliferate by cell shape deformations followed by spontaneous scission events, in a very similar manner to the process we have described for B. subtilis (Leaver et al., 2009; Mercier et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and citations.

claim: A minor reduction in FA synthesis prevents the growth of C. glutamicum and E. coli L-forms.
source: Additionally, as previously observed for B. subtilis, a minor reduction in FA synthesis prevented the growth of both C. glutamicum and E. coli L-forms, supporting the idea that all three L-forms divide by a similar mechanism based on an increased ratio of surface area to volume synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: All three L-forms (B. subtilis, C. glutamicum, and E. coli) divide by a similar mechanism based on an increased ratio of surface area to volume synthesis.
source: Additionally, as previously observed for B. subtilis, a minor reduction in FA synthesis prevented the growth of both C. glutamicum and E. coli L-forms, supporting the idea that all three L-forms divide by a similar mechanism based on an increased ratio of surface area to volume synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar effects of FA synthesis inhibition.

claim: Evolutionarily divergent bacteria with different envelope structures have retained a common primitive mode of proliferation when forced to grow in the absence of a cell wall.
source: Thus it appears that evolutionarily divergent bacteria, with different envelope structures (e.g. Gram-positive and Gram-negative), shape (e.g. rod vs sphere), and different modes of cell wall extension (e.g. lateral and apical) have retained a common primitive mode of proliferation when forced to grow in the absence of a cell wall.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar L-form properties across diverse species.

claim: The L-form mode of proliferation is similar to the mode of proliferation of simple vesicle systems independent of protein based machineries.
source: Interestingly, this mode of proliferation is strikingly similar to the mode of proliferation of simple vesicle systems independent of protein based machineries (Hanczyc et al., 2003; Budin et al., 2009; Terasawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanczyc et al., 2003; Budin et al., 2009; Terasawa et al., 2012.

claim: The L-form mode of proliferation could have been used by a common ancestor of the bacteria prior to the invention of the cell wall.
source: Therefore, our results strengthen the idea that the L-form mode of proliferation could have been used by a common ancestor of the bacteria prior to the invention of the cell wall, and are consistent with the notion that invention of the wall was a pivotal moment in the evolutionary divergence of the bacterial lineage (Errington, 2013).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by the experimental data and citation to Errington, 2013.

claim: Invention of the cell wall was a pivotal moment in the evolutionary divergence of the bacterial lineage.
source: Therefore, our results strengthen the idea that the L-form mode of proliferation could have been used by a common ancestor of the bacteria prior to the invention of the cell wall, and are consistent with the notion that invention of the wall was a pivotal moment in the evolutionary divergence of the bacterial lineage (Errington, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Errington, 2013.

claim: The simple mechanism of proliferation of L-forms may find application in attempts to design and engineer synthetic self-replicative systems or minimal cells.
source: Apart from its apparent importance for understanding an early step in the evolution of life, the simple mechanism of proliferation of L-forms may find application in attempts to design and engineer synthetic self-replicative systems, or minimal cells (Caspi and Dekker, 2014).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential applications, supported by citation to Caspi and Dekker, 2014.

claim: The ability to delete and then restore normally essential genes in L-forms offers a powerful new model system to investigate properties of the cell wall synthesis and cell division machineries.
source: The ability to delete and then restore normally essential genes in L-forms offers a powerful new model system with which to investigate important properties of the cell wall synthesis and cell division machineries, with implications for the discovery and development of novel antibacterials (Bugg et al., 2011; den Blaauwen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental capabilities demonstrated and supported by citations.

claim: MurA is inhibited by the antibiotic fosfomycin.
source: MurA, inhibited by the antibiotic FOS, and MurB catalyze the transformation of uridine diphosphate-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) into UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid (UDP-MurNAc).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge.

claim: The racemase Dal and the D-alanine ligase Ddl are both inhibited by the antibiotic D-cycloserine.
source: The racemase Dal and the D-alanine ligase Ddl, both of which are inhibited by the antibiotic DCS, are required to generate D-Ala-D-Ala.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge.

claim: MurA and MurB catalyze the transformation of UDP-GlcNAc into UDP-MurNAc.
source: MurA, inhibited by the antibiotic FOS, and MurB catalyze the transformation of uridine diphosphate-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) into UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid (UDP-MurNAc).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: Dal and Ddl are required to generate D-Ala-D-Ala.
source: The racemase Dal and the D-alanine ligase Ddl, both of which are inhibited by the antibiotic DCS, are required to generate D-Ala-D-Ala.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: D-Ala-D-Ala is incorporated into the UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide, requiring MurC, MurD, MurE, and MurF enzymes.
source: This is incorporated into the UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide, requiring MurC, MurD, MurE, and MurF enzymes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide is transferred to undecaprenyl pyrophosphate by MraY.
source: UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide is transferred to undecaprenyl pyrophosphate by MraY, and the addition of GlcNAc is catalyzed by MurG to form lipid II.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.

claim: The addition of GlcNAc to the MraY product is catalyzed by MurG to form lipid II.
source: UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide is transferred to undecaprenyl pyrophosphate by MraY, and the addition of GlcNAc is catalyzed by MurG to form lipid II.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis.
